section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department despatches, telegrams, and internal research memoranda from April to June 1937 detailing Japanese domestic political instability and foreign economic policy during the administration of General Senjuro Hayashi. The correspondence closely monitors the aftermath of the March 31 dissolution of the Diet, the April 30 general election in which opposition parties decisively defeated the military-backed government, and the aborted effort by conservative politicians to construct a pro-government rightist party. In addition, the documents extensively analyze Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's diplomatic platform and his economic thesis advocating international cooperation, unimpeded access to raw materials, and the avoidance of exclusionary trade blocs as alternatives to territorial aggression.

subfiles.about: Concluding section of a despatch transmitting a newspaper clipping on Diet member Yukio Ozaki's interpellations to the Japanese Government and official ministerial replies.
subfiles.summary: Clipping reports Ozaki's twelve interpellations on taxes, defense parity, the Anti-Comintern pact, mandated islands, and February 26; Sato denies returning islands to Germany, ministers call disarmament talks futile.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2346 from Tokyo: Questionnaire of Yukio Ozaki and Government Replies

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a Far Eastern Division memorandum regarding the Japanese political situation preceding the April 30 election.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: FE memo notes Japan marking time pending the April 30 election outcome.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum on Far Eastern Situation (Week Ending April 24, 1937)

subfiles.about: Reporting election returns indicating a major defeat for the Hayashi Cabinet and analyzing the Government's prospects for remaining in power.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the election as a clear Hayashi defeat, with opposition winning 354 seats and pro-government reduced to 30; the Cabinet plans to continue given no decisive mandate.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 122 from Tokyo on the Results of the General Election

subfiles.about: State Department summary and analysis of Embassy Despatch No. 2359 regarding the announced domestic and economic policies of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Turner summarizes Hayashi's vague eight-point program as reflecting continued military dominance toward semi-wartime regimentation, predicting strong Diet resistance forcing resignation, dissolution, or retreat.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on the Policies of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Detailed review and critique of the eight-point policy platform promulgated by the Hayashi Cabinet ahead of the April 30 general election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits and analyzes the official eight-point platform announced by Premier Hayashi following the dissolution of the Diet. The despatch examines proposed reforms in education, administrative machinery, armaments, industry, social insurance, and taxation, noting widespread domestic criticism of their vagueness and resemblance to Hirota Cabinet policies. Grew highlights the military's underlying goal of creating a Japanese variety of a totalitarian state through national mobilization and economic controls, while business and financial circles express deep apprehension over inflation and state regimentation. An enclosure reproduces The Japan Advertiser translation of the platform published on April 11, 1937.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2359 from Tokyo: Policies of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Summary of Embassy Despatch No. 2364 reporting on the failed political effort to create a rightist, pro-government party in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Turner notes Hayashi's Diet dissolution aimed at creating a rubber-stamp rightist party failed amid dictatorship fears and no willing top politicians, agreeing Hayashi miscalculated sentiment.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on the New Party Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive report on political maneuvers by politicians and the military to organize a new rightist party following the dissolution of the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the emergence and subsequent stalling of a movement among professional politicians to establish a rightist political party supporting the military-dominated Hayashi Cabinet. Prominent figures from established parties and minor factions were approached, and Premier Hayashi unsuccessfully sought Prince Fumimaro Konoye to lead the organization, while Finance Minister Toyotaro Yuki disavowed involvement. Public and newspaper resistance stiffened against the move over fears of an authoritarian dictatorship, forcing the Cabinet to abandon hope of organizing the party before the April 30 election. Grew observes that General Hayashi, by his own admission a soldier untrained in politics, fundamentally misjudged public hostility toward the arbitrary dissolution of the Diet.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2364 from Tokyo: New Party Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: Brief internal State Department routing and evaluation note on Tokyo Despatch No. 2367 concerning the pre-election campaign for the House of Representatives.
subfiles.summary: Brief memo notes Despatch 2367 describes pre-election campaign progress, now of little interest since written before voting.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on the Japanese Election Campaign

subfiles.about: Account of the political campaign, candidate registrations, and party manifestos leading up to the April 30 general election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the opening stages of the campaign for 466 seats in the House of Representatives following the March 31 dissolution of the Diet. He reviews candidate registrations, the Government's ambiguous eight-point platform, fierce counterattacks by the Seiyukai and Minseito against the Cabinet's unconstitutional behavior, and the energetic social-reform platform put forward by the Shakai Taishuto. Grew predicts that the major parties will fail to present a unified front, allowing the Hayashi Government to survive by dividing the opposition despite potential gains by the Shakai Taishuto and independents. Two newspaper clippings from The Japan Times and The Japan Advertiser containing candidate statistics and the Minseito appeal are enclosed.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2367 from Tokyo: Japanese Election Campaign to April 16, 1937

subfiles.about: Weekly intelligence briefing on political conditions in China and prospective courses of action for the Japanese Government following the April 30 election.
subfiles.summary: Weekly FE memo reports no major China news; Japan's election occurred April 30 with results pending and outlines four possible Hayashi responses to an adverse vote.
subfiles.title: Weekly Memorandum: The Situation in the Far East (May 1, 1937)

subfiles.about: Detailed analytical study tracing the escalating confrontation between the Japanese military hierarchy and parliamentary parties during 1937.
subfiles.summary: This State Department study reviews the political crisis precipitated by Kunimatsu Hamada's confrontation with War Minister Terauchi in January 1937, which triggered the collapse of the Hirota Cabinet. It examines the military's obstruction of General Ugaki's attempt to form a cabinet, General Hayashi's assumption of the premiership, budget debates, and veteran liberal Yukio Ozaki's outspoken parliamentary attacks against militarism and the anti-Comintern pact. The report further discusses Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's moderate diplomatic rhetoric, the sudden dissolution of the Diet on March 31, and the emergence of fascist tendencies within the Kwantung Army under General Itagaki, concluding with an analysis of structural differences between Japanese militarism and European totalitarian dictatorships.
subfiles.title: Report on Japan: The Clash Between the Army and the Political Parties

subfiles.about: Analysis of the April 30 Japanese parliamentary election results and their implications for military influence and cabinet survival.
subfiles.summary: Turner notes the opposition's clear election win repudiated the Cabinet specifically rather than military rule generally, suggesting a pragmatic Cabinet-Diet compromise to avoid crisis.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Parliamentary Elections in Japan

subfiles.about: Weekly intelligence briefing covering the Japanese election aftermath and Foreign Minister Sato's statements on China policy.
subfiles.summary: Weekly FE memo notes Hayashi intends to stay despite the opposition's majority; Sato proposed improving China relations by settling minor issues first, questioning military tolerance for conciliation.
subfiles.title: Weekly Memorandum: The Situation in the Far East (May 8, 1937)

subfiles.about: Reporting addresses by Premier Hayashi and Foreign Minister Sato before the Conference of Prefectural Governors on domestic and foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits Sato's governors' conference address on China, Soviet Far East, Britain, U.S., and Germany ties, urging cultural/economic cooperation with China, caution with Soviets, and fair treatment of foreigners.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 131 from Tokyo on Addresses to the Conference of Prefectural Governors

subfiles.about: Assessment of Tokyo Despatch No. 2390 and Foreign Minister Sato's economic philosophy regarding international resource allocation and trade.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine reviews Sato's economic views on removing trade barriers, citing his Paris lecture, House's 'New Deal Among Nations' article, and plans to protest raw-material monopolies before the League.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Foreign Minister Sato's Basic Economic Views

subfiles.about: Comprehensive analysis of Foreign Minister Sato's international economic theories, accompanied by supporting articles and speeches.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides an in-depth analysis of Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's convictions that international peace depends upon equitable access to raw materials and open markets rather than territorial aggression. Following conversations between Sato and Embassy officer Cabot Coville, Grew examines Sato's intellectual alignment with Colonel Edward M. House's thesis in 'Wanted—A New Deal Among Nations' and Professor Teijiro Ueda's population studies, contrasting Sato's restrained, trade-oriented solutions with House's calls for territorial readjustments. The despatch includes enclosures comprising a Japan Advertiser clipping on Sato's planned appeal to the League of Nations raw materials committee, and a Japanese Foreign Office reprint and translation of Colonel House's 1935 Liberty article.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2390 from Tokyo: Foreign Minister Sato's Basic Economic Views
